b: I love reading old articles. This usually means reading the classics of the medical literature. In the early days of Sensible Medicine, I started a series called My Favorite Articles. I only got through four papers before getting distracted:
Caffeine Intake and the Risk of First-Trimester Spontaneous Abortion
Postmenopausal Estrogen and Progestin Use and the Risk of Cardiovascular Disease
Prevention of Coronary Heart Disease with Pravastatin in Men with Hypercholesterolemia
Self-reported Cannabis Use as a Risk Factor for Schizophrenia in Swedish Conscripts of 1969: Historical Cohort Study
I need to get back to that series.
Sensible Medicine is a reader-supported Substack. If you appreciate our work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

We also recently dissected the 2004 article Coronary-Artery Revascularization before Elective Major Vascular Surgery on This Fortnight in Medicine XXXIII. It was fun to see how well a 22-year-old study holds up.

I also love reading “thought pieces” from earlier eras: Perspectives, Piece of My Mind, On Being A Doctor. Of the hundreds that attendings or older colleagues handed me, there are a dozen or so that I read, loved, and saved. These essays reside in a (real-life paper) folder in my office, a little crinkled, some coffee-stained. A few of my favorites:
The Chagrin Factor and Qualitative Decision Analysis by Alvan Feinstein (1985)
The Art of Pimping by Frederick Brancati (1989)
The Quick Physical Exam by Robert Hirschtick (2016)

After a particularly tough clinic recently, I went back to an article I was given a few times during training: Taking Care of the Hateful Patient. I read it to see if I could learn anything, 35 years after it was first given to me.

James Groves, a psychiatrist at MGH, published this article in 1978. He must have been early in his career, and the publication must have been a coup. Reading it is like venturing into another world. Most striking is the language. The writing would be considered insensitive and inappropriate in 2026. If submitted today, it would be a guaranteed desk reject, maybe with a letter to your chair asking, “Who is this guy?”

To give a sense of the language, Groves describes four types of hateful patients. Instead of identifying different types of personality disorders, he refers to the patients as dependent clingers, entitled demanders, manipulative help-rejecters, and self-destructive deniers. Terrifically descriptive, yes; acceptable ways of describing patients today, probably not.

I am not criticizing Dr. Groves in any way. He wrote a brave and influential paper back in ’78. I am sure nothing I have written will be the subject of a Substack (descendant) essay in 50 years. I am also sure that, if he were to rewrite the article today, he would state things differently.

Besides the language, the article is notable for its lack of data. Patients are grouped into four types, recommendations are made about creating therapeutic relationships, articles are cited, but the recommendations are based on experience alone. Again, this is not a criticism. In a way, things are worse now. A similar article today would include bad observational data, certainly worse than no data at all.
The paper is interesting, a good read, but maybe not that helpful
We can’t expect one paper to offer a panacea for the most difficult doctor-patient relationships. Groves recommends how to handle relationships with each of the four patient types.

people who escalate from mild and appropriate requests for reassurance to repeated, perfervid, incarcerating cries for explanation, affection, analgesics, sedatives and all forms of attention imaginable.
How is that for some killer prose; I told you that this article doesn’t sound anything like a paper written in 2026! His recommendation for caring for the dependent clinger is to tell him/her,
as early in the relationship as possible, and as tactfully and firmly as possible, that the physician has not only human limits to knowledge and skill but also limitations to time and stamina.

The entitled demander is the patient who “use(s) intimidation, devaluation and guilt-induction to place the doctor in the role of the inexhaustible supply depot.” For these patients, Groves recommends supporting “the entitlement but to rechannel it in the direction of the indicated regimen.”
The manipulative help-rejecter Groves describes thus:

They appear to feel that no regimen will help. Appearing almost smugly satisfied, they return again and again to the office or clinic to report that, once again, the regimen did not work. Their pessimism and tenacious nay-saying appear to increase in direct proportion to the physician’s efforts and enthusiasm. When one of their symptoms is relieved, another mysteriously appears in its place. Apparently, what is sought is not relief of symptoms. What is sought is an undivorcible marriage with an inexhaustible caregiver.
The recommendations here are “limits on unrealistic expectations, limits on demanding hostility and — most of all — repeated appeals to entitlement are again invoked.”

Last are the self-destructive deniers, those patients with “unconsciously self-murderous behaviors, such as the continued drinking of a patient with esophageal varices and hepatic failure.” Even Groves seems at a loss with these people; he begins his discussion:

What the physician can do to help self-destructive deniers is quite limited. The starting point for the care of such a patient is to recognize without shame or self-blame that they provoke in their caregivers the fervent wish that they would die and “get it over with.”

I saw flickering reflections of some of my most troublesome relationships in Groves’ article. On the day that I returned to the article, I was working to categorize a specific patient who had troubled me in clinic. Actual people, however, are more complex than the article’s archetypes. And, as a primary care doctor, I don’t have the time or the wherewithal to identify the types and construct perfect relationships; I practice experience-based muddling.
It is telling that I was given this paper more than once

Maybe what I got most from this paper, when I was first handed it in 1992 and now, is that all doctors care for patients who make us feel like failures. We all need help. My teachers who referenced the Groves’ paper were letting me know this.

Doctors, not without reason, are not universally loved. We can be insensitive, distant, and inattentive. If I looked at comments on some of my posts on X, I am sure I could come up with other adjectives.

Although some of the hate is well deserved, some of it is an unavoidable product of doing a nearly impossible job. Think of the people in your life you find insufferable; the woman on the bus behaving terribly, the man at the diner berating the waitress, your high school nemesis. Now imagine dedicating yourself to working with that person, overcoming all their baggage and anxieties, to do the best you can for them.

Taking Care of the Hateful Patient makes it clear that the article isn’t about caring for a mildly difficult person, or someone a doctor might handle poorly because of countertransference. These are the patients who everybody would struggle with. This is why this article was passed to me every couple of years.

I would be on an inpatient team, or I would be seeing someone in clinic, precepted by an attending, and we would be working with a patient who we truly dreaded seeing. Someone we could do nothing right for, who made us feel like failures and undermined our best efforts.
These were the times that my senior would ask, “Have you read the Groves paper?”

Caring for patients is a privilege. It is also a privilege to have doctors from the past to counsel you from another time. Whether reading a well-designed observational study, a brilliantly conducted clinical trial, or a well-reasoned thought piece, there is so much experience to learn from – even if what you are learning is that the job is hard.
